prompt.context: Your client is CarCo, a mechanics and auto parts company in the MidWest. CarCo provides automotive services to customers (tires, oil changes, engine repair, etc.). The business is family owned and operated, and has historically generated $25 million in profits annually. Recently, the business has experienced far lower profits than usual, namely $10 million. While the business is still profitable, a similar drop in profits would be catastrophic. You have been hired to assess the root cause of decreased profits and help turn the business around.
prompt.question: What is the root cause of CarCo's profit decline from $25M to $10M, and how would you recommend turning the business around?

clarifying_info.q: Does CarCo operate in multiple locations?
clarifying_info.a: CarCo only operates in the MidWest and you can assume it is a single location.

clarifying_info.q: What products or services does CarCo offer?
clarifying_info.a: CarCo mainly offers three products/services: regular tires, oil changes, and engine overhauls.

clarifying_info.q: How long has the profit decline been occurring?
clarifying_info.a: The profit decline is only observed in the last few years.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific financial target or timeline for improvement?
clarifying_info.a: No specific financial target or timeline. CarCo just wants to identify the root cause and find solutions to these problems.

exhibits.title: Revenue Streams Question
exhibits.shows: Slide posing the question: given that the company's cost structure has remained constant and there are no external market factors, what revenue streams would you expect this mechanic to have?

exhibits.title: Product/Service Pricing and Margin Table
exhibits.shows: A table listing CarCo's three products/services with their prices and profit margins at 50%.
exhibits.data: Regular Tire: Price $10, Profit Margin $5; Oil Change: Price $30, Profit Margin $15; Engine Overhaul: Price $200, Profit Margin $100. Total quantity sold historically constant at 1 million. Prices have not changed.

exhibits.title: Cause of Profit Decline — Setup
exhibits.shows: Slide framing the profit-decline explanation and asking the candidate to explain what happened and how to increase profits.

framework: 1. Market issues (external): declining market for mechanic services due to shift to renewable energy / fewer vehicles; cars needing fewer repairs; rise of DIY repair

2. Revenue decline for CarCo: (A) Prices have fallen — lower willingness to pay, price wars, economic hardship; (B) Quantity sold has dropped — competitor market-share gains, quality deterioration, slower turnaround
3. Cost increase for CarCo: (A) Fixed costs — facility rental, utilities, equipment, SG&A; (B) Variable costs — labor/recruiting/training, car parts (incl. software), timing costs for lengthy repairs

Business insight: A very strong answer hypothesizes the root cause early (e.g., cost changes of $15M seem unlikely for a mechanic, so focus on revenue/mix); leverages real-world context such as the shift to electric vehicles.

questions.prompt: Q1 — Identify Revenue Streams: The company's cost structure has remained constant and there are no external market factors. What revenue streams would you expect this mechanic to have?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm across three buckets: (1) Products — hardware (tires, engines, brakes, alternators), software (speakers, radios, touchscreens, chargers), miscellaneous (oil, coolant); (2) Services — yearly inspections, winterizing, oil changes, post-accident repair, scrapping; (3) Passive income — investments, property.

questions.prompt: Q2 — Product/Service Mix: Given the pricing table (Exhibit 2), total quantity sold has remained constant at 1 million and prices have not changed, yet profits fell from $25M to $10M. Explain what happened and suggest how to increase profits.
questions.guidance: The profit decline is explained by a mix shift: customers have purchased proportionally more low-margin tires and oil changes, and proportionally fewer high-margin engine overhauls. This is a product-mix / revenue-mix problem, not a price or volume problem. Strong candidates quantify the implied mix shift. Revenue increase suggestions: (1) expand customer base or open additional locations; (2) broaden product offering and create bundled packages to increase spend per customer; (3) reduce price of engine overhauls to compete — competitors may have undercut CarCo; (4) if market is moving to DIY, sell engines without service or expand into DIY kits; (5) marketing campaign or community promotions.

math.setup: Historical profit = $25M on 1M units. Current profit = $10M on 1M units (same prices). Implied weighted-average profit per unit historically = $25; currently = $10. The only change is the mix across three products: Regular Tire ($5 margin), Oil Change ($15 margin), Engine Overhaul ($100 margin). A large shift from Engine Overhaul toward the lower-margin items accounts for the $15M profit drop.
steps: Let x = number of engine overhauls sold currently vs. historically. Each engine overhaul lost = $100 margin lost. To lose $15M, roughly 150,000 fewer engine overhauls sold (offset partially by more tires/oil changes at lower margins).

Example check: if historically 200K engine overhauls @ $100 = $20M and 800K tires/oil @ avg $6.25 = $5M → $25M total; if currently 50K engine overhauls @ $100 = $5M and 950K tires/oil @ avg ~$5.26 = $5M → $10M total — directionally consistent.
math.answer: Profit declined because the product mix shifted heavily from high-margin engine overhauls ($100/unit) toward low-margin tires ($5) and oil changes ($15), while total unit volume and prices stayed flat.

questions.prompt: Q3 — Strategy Risks: CarCo wants to add 'Star Tires' to its product line, selling at $25 with a 60% profit margin. What are the risks?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates cover multiple risk dimensions: (1) Cannibalization — Star Tire buyers may substitute away from regular tires, not represent incremental volume; (2) Customer fit — existing customers are already migrating away from expensive products; are Star Tire shoppers the current customer base or new customers?; (3) Brand — as a family-owned shop, selling premium tires may require a quality/service upgrade or risk brand confusion; (4) Permanence — Star Tires may be a fad, or if they last longer they may require less frequent replacement and less maintenance, reducing long-run revenue; (5) Execution — stable supplier required, sufficient inventory, mechanics trained to install.

recommendation: Profits have fallen 60% (from $25M to $10M) due to a sharp drop in engine overhaul sales — the highest-margin product at $100 per unit. Increased sales of tires and oil changes have been insufficient to compensate.
CarCo should reprice engine overhauls competitively by benchmarking against local mechanics and consider modest price reductions to regain volume.
CarCo should evaluate adding Star Tires (60% margin vs. current 50%), which could improve blended margins if cannibalization is limited.
risks: Lowering engine overhaul prices may further reduce profits if overall demand for engine repairs is structurally declining (e.g., more reliable modern vehicles, shift to EVs).
Adding Star Tires risks cannibalizing regular tire sales, especially if the customer base is price-sensitive.
Expanding the product line requires supply chain, inventory, and mechanic capability investments.
next_steps: Conduct competitive pricing analysis for engine overhauls in the MidWest market.
Run a detailed cost-benefit and cannibalization analysis before committing to Star Tires.
Explore bundled service packages (e.g., tire + oil change) to increase revenue per customer visit.
Assess whether a targeted marketing campaign can shift customer behavior back toward higher-margin services.
